subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look around you right now. The air you are breathing, the soil outside your door, the skin on the back of your hand, and even the inside of your own stomach are all crowded with living things that are far too small for your eyes to see. We call these tiny living things microorganisms, which simply means 'very small organisms'. In this unit you will discover that although a single microorganism is smaller than a speck of dust, together they are among the most powerful and important living things on Earth.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 0893 — Stage 7 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, working at your own pace with help from your AI tutor and your teacher, you will be able to:
Explain what a microorganism is and why a microscope is needed to see one.
Name and describe the main kinds of microorganism: bacteria, fungi (including yeast and mould), protozoa and algae, and explain why viruses are treated differently.
Describe how a single microorganism grows into a colony that is large enough to see.
Distinguish between microorganisms that are useful to people and those that are harmful.
Construct and interpret food chains and food webs, using arrows to show the direction of energy transfer.
Classify organisms as producers, consumers, herbivores, carnivores, predators, prey or decomposers.
Explain how microorganisms cause decay, and describe the important role of decomposers in returning nutrients to the soil.
Investigate how temperature and moisture affect the rate of decay, and draw a conclusion from your results.
Discuss the role of microorganisms in food, in health and in the wider environment, including in your own community.

concepts.title: What Is a Microorganism?
concepts.explanation:
A microorganism is a living organism that is so small you cannot see it clearly without a microscope. The word is built from two parts: 'micro', meaning very small, and 'organism', meaning a living thing. Like every other living thing — like you, like a camel, like an acacia tree — microorganisms are made of cells. The difference is size. Many microorganisms are made of just a single cell, and that one cell is so tiny that thousands of them together would still be smaller than a grain of sand.

It helps to picture the scale. A cell in your own body is already too small to see on its own. A single bacterium is far smaller still — many times smaller than one of your cells. That is why, for thousands of years, human beings had no idea these creatures existed. People saw milk turn sour, bread rise, and wounds go bad, but they could not see the living things causing it. Only when the microscope was invented could scientists finally look closely enough to discover a hidden living world.

There are several different kinds of microorganism. The main groups you will study are bacteria, microscopic fungi, protozoa and algae. Viruses are also extremely small, but scientists usually treat them separately, and you will soon learn why. Let us take each group in turn.

Bacteria are everywhere — in the air, in the soil, in water, on every surface, on your skin and inside your gut. The word 'bacteria' is plural; a single one is called a bacterium. Each bacterium is made of just one cell, and that cell is much smaller than an animal cell or a plant cell. As you read earlier, you could line up about 1000 bacteria end to end in the space between two millimetre marks on your ruler. Bacteria have a cell wall, but unlike plant and animal cells they have no nucleus.

It is easy to think that all bacteria are 'germs' that make us ill, but this is a mistake. Most bacteria are completely harmless, and many are extremely useful. Right now, helpful bacteria are living in your digestive system, helping you to break down your food. Other helpful bacteria turn milk into yoghurt and into the fermented camel milk that many families across the Horn of Africa enjoy. Only a small number of bacteria cause disease.

Fungi (a single one is a fungus) are not always microorganisms. Many fungi, such as the mushrooms and toadstools you might see pushing up from damp ground after rain, are large and easy to see without any microscope. But a mushroom is only a small part of the fungus — the part that makes new spores. Most of the fungus is a tangle of very fine threads spreading through the soil or through a dead log, so thin that you would need a microscope to see them.

Some fungi never make mushrooms at all. They are made of single cells, so these ones truly are microorganisms. The most famous example is yeast. The dusty, powdery bloom you sometimes see on the skin of grapes or dates is made of millions of yeast cells feeding on the sugar in the fruit. Yeast is a single-celled fungus, and under a microscope you can watch tiny buds growing out of the cells — that is how yeast makes more of itself. Mould, the fuzzy growth on old bread or a forgotten mango, is another fungus; it grows as fine threads and is a very common decomposer.

Did You Know? The bubbles that make bread and canjeero rise are made by yeast. As the yeast feeds on sugar in the dough, it produces a gas that puffs the dough up. Fungi are neither plants nor animals. They belong to a kingdom of living things all of their own.

Viruses are even smaller than bacteria — so small that ordinary microscopes cannot show them at all. A virus is not made of a cell. It is a tiny particle, just a small package of instructions wrapped in a protein coat. Because it is not a cell and cannot feed, grow or reproduce on its own, most scientists do not call a virus a true microorganism, and many do not even call it fully 'alive'. A virus can only make copies of itself by getting inside the living cell of another organism and taking over that cell's machinery. The illnesses called colds, flu (influenza), measles and COVID are all caused by viruses.

If you put a single drop of pond water or river water under a microscope, you would see it teeming with life. Some of the tiny creatures are protozoa — single-celled microorganisms whose cells are like animal cells, often moving about actively as they hunt for even smaller food. One kind of protozoan is very important to your community: it causes malaria, and it is carried from person to person by mosquitoes. Other tiny organisms in the water are algae — single-celled microorganisms whose cells are like plant cells. Like plants, algae are green and can use sunlight to make their own food. The green tinge you sometimes see in still water is made of countless algae.
concepts.example: [*] Remember! A microorganism is any living thing too small to see clearly without a microscope. The main kinds are bacteria, fungi (including yeast and mould), protozoa and algae. Viruses are even smaller and are treated separately because they are not cells and cannot live on their own. Most microorganisms are harmless or helpful. Only a few cause disease.

concepts.title: Growing Microorganisms into Colonies
concepts.explanation:
A single microorganism is far too small to see. So how do scientists study them? The trick is to let them grow. When a single bacterium or a single fungus cell is given warmth, moisture and food, it divides in two. Then each of those divides again, and again, and again. In only a day or two, one invisible cell becomes a colony of millions of cells — and a colony is big enough to see with your naked eye, as a small spot or patch.

In a laboratory, scientists grow colonies on a special jelly called agar jelly, poured into a shallow round dish with a lid called a Petri dish. The agar jelly contains nutrients — the food the microorganisms need. Before use, both the dish and the jelly must be sterile, which means every living thing on them has already been killed. If the dish were not sterile, unwanted microorganisms would already be growing there and would spoil the experiment. When the dish is left open to the air for a few minutes, microorganisms floating in the air settle onto the jelly, and after a few days each one has grown into a visible colony.

You can even tell the two main groups apart by looking. Colonies of bacteria usually have smooth, shiny edges, while colonies of fungi are usually fuzzy or furry with rough edges, because the fungus grows as fine threads. In the Experiments file you will grow your own colonies safely at home, using nothing more than a slice of bread — no laboratory needed.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The word 'sterile' means totally free of all living things. Doctors sterilise their instruments so that no harmful microorganisms are passed to a patient. This is exactly why a nurse boils water or uses very hot steam to clean equipment — heat kills microorganisms.

concepts.title: Useful and Harmful Microorganisms
concepts.explanation:
Because a few microorganisms cause serious disease, people often fear all of them. But the truth is more interesting and more balanced: microorganisms are among the most useful living things we have, and human life would be impossible without them.

Think of your own kitchen. Bacteria turn fresh milk into yoghurt and into the sour fermented camel milk that many families drink. They do this by changing the sugar in the milk into acid, which is what gives yoghurt its sharp, pleasant taste and its thick texture. Yeast, a fungus, makes dough rise so that bread and canjeero become soft and light instead of hard and flat. In the wider world, decomposer bacteria and fungi in the savanna soil break down dead plants and animal dung and release their nutrients back into the ground, so that fresh grass and acacia trees can grow — which in turn feeds the goats, camels and wild animals. Inside your own body, friendly bacteria in your gut help you digest food and keep harmful microbes out.

Some microorganisms, though, are harmful. When bacteria or mould grow on food we meant to eat, they spoil it and can make us ill if we eat it. This is why food left out in the heat goes bad so quickly, and why we must be careful with meat, milk and cooked rice in a hot climate. A small number of microorganisms cause disease directly. The protozoan that causes malaria is spread by mosquito bites and remains one of the most serious health problems in East Africa, especially for young children. Dirty water can carry bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid, and other bacteria cause tuberculosis. Viruses cause the flu, measles and many other illnesses.

The good news is that simple actions protect us. Boiling drinking water kills the microorganisms in it. Washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet stops harmful microbes spreading from hands to food. Cooking food thoroughly and keeping it covered and cool slows down spoilage. Sleeping under a bed net and clearing away still water where mosquitoes breed reduces the risk of malaria. In Islam, keeping clean is highly valued — Muslims wash carefully before each prayer, and cleanliness is described as part of faith. Science shows us exactly why this care with cleanliness and clean water keeps whole communities healthy.
concepts.example: [*] A Balanced View Useful microorganisms: make yoghurt and fermented milk, raise bread and canjeero, help digestion, and recycle nutrients in the soil. Harmful microorganisms: spoil food, and a few cause diseases such as malaria, cholera and the flu. Good hygiene, clean water, cooking food well and covering food protect us from the harmful ones.

concepts.title: Food Chains - How Energy Flows
concepts.explanation:
To understand where microorganisms fit into the natural world, you first need to understand how energy flows through all living things. Every living thing needs energy — to move, to grow, to stay warm, to reproduce. When Hassan eats a plate of bariis (rice) with goat meat, that food gives him energy for the day. But where did that energy come from in the first place?

The answer is the Sun. Almost all the energy used by living things on Earth begins as sunlight. Green plants — and algae — can capture the energy in sunlight and use it to make their own food. Because they produce food from sunlight, plants are called producers. Some of the energy from the sunlight becomes stored in the plant's roots, stems, leaves, grains and fruits.

When an animal eats the plant, it takes in that stored food and so takes in the energy too. This passing of energy from one living thing to the next is called energy transfer. Animals cannot make their own food, so they must eat ready-made food. For this reason all animals are called consumers. We can show the path of the energy by drawing a food chain, using arrows to show the direction the energy flows.

For example, here is a simple food chain from the savanna:

Read the arrows as 'is eaten by' or, better, as 'energy flows to'. The grass is the producer; it captured energy from the Sun. The goat eats the grass and gains that energy. The lion eats the goat and gains the energy in turn. Notice that the arrows always point in the direction the energy travels — from the food to the eater — never backwards. A very common mistake is to draw the arrow the wrong way, from the eater to its food. Always ask yourself: which way is the energy flowing?

Scientists use special words to describe each organism's role:

Producer — the first organism in the chain; it makes its own food from sunlight. Grass and acacia trees are producers.

Consumer — any organism that eats others. Every animal is a consumer.

Herbivore — a consumer that eats only plants, such as a camel, a goat or a springbok.

Carnivore — a consumer that eats only other animals, such as a lion or a cheetah.

Predator — an animal that catches, kills and eats other animals.

Prey — an animal that is caught and eaten by a predator.

The same animal can have more than one label. A leopard is a consumer, a carnivore and a predator all at once. A zebra it hunts is a consumer, a herbivore, and also prey. Learning to apply these labels correctly is an important skill in this unit.

Did You Know? Every food chain starts with a producer, because producers are the only living things that can capture new energy from the Sun. Along the Indian Ocean coast near Mombasa and Kismaayo, tiny floating algae are the producers that begin nearly every ocean food chain, feeding the small fish that feed the larger fish that people catch.

In the real world, very few animals eat only one kind of food, and very few plants are eaten by only one kind of animal. A cheetah might eat a springbok or a young zebra. A springbok might be eaten by a cheetah, a leopard or a hyena. When we join many food chains together to show all these connections, we get a food web. A food web is a much more realistic picture of a habitat than a single food chain.

Imagine a savanna food web near Garissa. Grass and acacia trees are the producers. Springbok and zebra eat the grass and the acacia leaves — they are herbivores. Termites also eat grass, and aardvarks eat the termites. Cheetahs, leopards and hyenas hunt the springbok and zebra. From one such diagram you can trace many different food chains, each one starting at a producer and following the arrows up to a top predator.
concepts.example: A food web is a model — a simplified picture that scientists use to represent something complicated. Like any model, it is useful but not perfect. A real savanna has thousands of species, and no drawing could ever show every single feeding relationship. Still, a food web helps us understand how the living things in one place depend on one another. If one link is removed — say, disease kills most of the zebra — every animal connected to them in the web is affected.

concepts.title: Microorganisms and Decay
concepts.explanation:
Now we can bring microorganisms into the story of energy and food. Think of a mango that has been left on the table for a week. It becomes soft, then brown, then covered in fuzzy patches. Each patch is a colony of millions of cells of microscopic fungi — this is mould, and we say the mango has become mouldy. The microorganisms have changed the mango; they have made it decay, or rot.

Organisms that make things decay are called decomposers. The most important decomposers are certain bacteria and fungi. A decomposer feeds on dead material by breaking it down, and as it feeds, the material rots. The mango is made of material that was produced by a living plant. Any substance made by a living thing — fruit, bread, wood, leather, paper, dead leaves, dead animals — is called organic matter. Decomposers can break down organic matter, but they cannot break down things that were never alive, such as rock, glass, plastic or metal.

At first, decay seems like nothing but a nuisance. No one wants to eat a rotten mango, and food spoiling in the heat is a real problem in a warm climate. But decay is one of the most important processes on the whole planet, and without it life could not continue.

Think about what would happen if nothing ever decayed. Every leaf that ever fell, every animal that ever died, every pile of dung dropped by a camel or an elephant would simply stay there forever. The savanna would be buried metres deep in dead plants, dead animals and waste. Instead, decomposers get to work. As bacteria and fungi break down dead bodies and dung, they release the valuable nutrients locked inside back into the soil. Plants then take up these nutrients through their roots and use them to grow. More plant growth means more food for the herbivores, which means more food for the carnivores. In this way, decomposers return nutrients to the soil and keep the whole web of life going.

You can see this yourself. Where a camel or a cow has left dung in a field, fungi grow on the dung, break it down, and the grass nearby grows greener and taller than the grass further away. The dung, broken down by decomposers, has fed the soil. This is exactly the idea behind composting: when a family collects fruit peelings, vegetable scraps and dead leaves into a pit or heap and lets decomposers break them down, the result is rich compost that makes garden soil fertile — turning waste into food for plants.

Did You Know? Almost all decomposers are microorganisms. Fungi and bacteria are the most important of all. In caring for the earth and not wasting what it provides, a Muslim acts as a khalifah, a steward or caretaker of the land. Composting kitchen waste instead of throwing it away is one small, practical way of doing this.

How Temperature and Moisture Affect Decay

Decomposers are living things, so the speed at which they work depends on the conditions around them. Two conditions matter most: warmth and moisture (water). Like most living things, decomposers grow and feed faster when it is warm and there is plenty of water. That is why food goes bad far more quickly on a hot day than on a cool one, and why bread kept in a refrigerator stays fresh much longer than bread left on the counter. It is also why moist bread grows mould faster than dry bread.

This everyday science is the reason for many of the ways people keep food safe. Drying meat and fish in the sun removes the water that decomposers need, so the food lasts longer. Keeping milk and cooked food cool slows the microorganisms down. Salting and smoking food make it harder for microorganisms to grow. In the Experiments file you will test these ideas for yourself by comparing how quickly bread decays in a warm place and in a cool place, and in moist and dry conditions.
concepts.example: [*] Remember! Decomposers (mostly bacteria and fungi) break down dead organic matter and cause decay. Decay returns nutrients to the soil so that plants can grow — this keeps all life going. Decomposers work faster in warm, moist conditions and slower in cold, dry conditions. We slow down harmful decay of our food by keeping it cool, dry, covered and clean.

concepts.title: Placing Decomposers into Food Webs
concepts.explanation:
You have learned that food webs show how energy flows from producers to consumers. But those webs left something out: what happens to the energy and nutrients when a plant or animal dies? This is where decomposers complete the picture.

Decomposers feed on almost every organism after it dies, and on the waste that living animals leave behind. When they do this, energy from the dead organism is transferred into the decomposer — just as energy was transferred when a goat ate grass. So decomposers are a special kind of consumer: they consume dead organisms and waste rather than living food. They are never producers, because they do not make their own food from sunlight.

To add decomposers to a food web properly, you would need to draw an arrow from every single plant and animal in the web to the decomposers, because eventually every organism dies and is broken down. That would make the diagram very crowded, which is why decomposers are often left off simple food webs. But they are always there, doing the vital work of recycling. Here is a small food web with decomposers included:
concepts.example: banana -> fruit bat -> python, and both the fruit bat and the python, when they die, are broken down by microorganisms (decomposers), which return nutrients to the soil where the banana plant grows. The circle is complete: nutrients flow from the soil, into plants, through animals, and back to the soil again.

methods.title: Growing Mould on Bread (Colonies You Can See)
methods.example: Hypothesis prompt: Write what you think will happen to a piece of moist bread left in a warm place for a week. What will you see, and when?
steps: Lightly dampen both slices of bread with a few drops of water. Do not soak them.
Leave both slices uncovered on a clean plate for about 30 minutes so microorganisms from the air can settle on them.
Place each slice in its own plastic bag or container and seal it firmly. Once sealed, do NOT open it again.
Label each bag with your name and the date.
Put both bags in a warm place away from direct sunlight, such as a kitchen shelf.

methods.title: Making Yoghurt with Helpful Bacteria
methods.example: Hypothesis prompt: Predict what the milk will look, feel and taste like after one night in a warm place. How will it be different from fresh milk?
steps: Ask an adult to help you wash the container with boiling water, then let it cool. This kills unwanted microorganisms.
Warm the milk until it is pleasantly warm to the touch — not hot. Ask an adult to help.
Pour the warm milk into the clean container.
Stir in the tablespoon of yoghurt. This adds the living bacteria that will turn the milk into yoghurt.
Cover the container and wrap it in a blanket to keep it warm. Leave it undisturbed for 6 to 10 hours (overnight works well).

methods.title: Does Temperature Affect Decay?
methods.example: Hypothesis prompt: Complete this sentence: 'I think the bread in the ______ place will decay faster because ______.'
steps: Dampen both slices with the SAME small amount of water so this variable is kept the same.
Seal each slice in its own bag and label them 'Warm' and 'Cool' with the date.
Put the 'Warm' bag in a warm place and the 'Cool' bag in the refrigerator or coolest place you have.
Keep both bags SEALED for the whole experiment.
Each day for 5 to 7 days, look at both slices through the bags and record how much mould has grown.

steps: Observe carefully and record what you see.
Compare your result with your hypothesis.

workedExamples.title: Worked example
workedExamples.prompt: Some questions in this unit ask you to organise results and calculate a mean (an average). Work through these carefully — every step is shown.
workedExamples.solution:
Worked Example 1: Building a Food Chain

Question: A chicken eats grain from a maize plant. Amina eats the chicken. Draw a food chain and label each organism.

Step 1 — Find the producer. The maize plant makes its own food using sunlight, so it is the producer. It goes first.

Step 2 — Follow who eats whom. The chicken eats the maize grain. Amina eats the chicken.

workedExamples.title: 1: Building a Food Chain
workedExamples.prompt: Question: A chicken eats grain from a maize plant. Amina eats the chicken. Draw a food chain and label each organism.
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Find the producer. The maize plant makes its own food using sunlight, so it is the producer. It goes first.

Step 2 — Follow who eats whom. The chicken eats the maize grain. Amina eats the chicken.

Step 3 — Draw the chain with arrows pointing in the direction energy flows:

maize plant -> chicken -> Amina

workedExamples.title: 2: Calculating a Mean
workedExamples.prompt: Question: Khadija measures the length of five grass leaves growing next to cow dung: 11 cm, 13 cm, 9 cm, 12 cm and 8 cm. What is the mean (average) length?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Add up all the values. 11 + 13 + 9 + 12 + 8 = 53 cm.

Step 2 — Count how many values there are. There are 5 leaves.

Step 3 — Divide the total by the number of values. 53 divided by 5 = 10.6 cm.

Answer: The mean length of the grass leaves next to the cow dung is 10.6 cm. To compare, if the five leaves far from dung measured 9, 10, 6, 7 and 9 cm, their total is 41 cm and their mean is 41 divided by 5 = 8.2 cm. The grass near the dung is taller on average, which fits the idea that decomposers broke the dung down and returned nutrients to the soil, helping the grass grow.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: A microorganism is best described as: (a) any small animal; (b) a living thing too small to see without a microscope; (c) a type of insect; (d) a non-living particle.
workedExamples.solution: 1 (b) A microorganism is a living thing too small to see clearly without a microscope.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a single-celled fungus? (a) a mushroom; (b) a bacterium; (c) yeast; (d) a virus.
workedExamples.solution: 2 (c) Yeast is a single-celled fungus. A mushroom is a large fungus, not single-celled.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Bacteria differ from plant and animal cells because they: (a) are much larger; (b) have no cell wall; (c) have no nucleus; (d) contain chlorophyll.
workedExamples.solution: 3 (c) Bacteria have a cell wall but no nucleus, unlike plant and animal cells.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Why are viruses usually NOT called true microorganisms? (a) they are too large; (b) they are not made of cells and cannot reproduce on their own; (c) they are always harmless; (d) they only live in soil.
workedExamples.solution: 4 (b) A virus is not a cell and can only reproduce inside a living cell, so it is treated separately.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8

activities.title: Growing Mould on Bread (Colonies You Can See)
activities.materials: 2 slices of bread (any kind); A little clean water and a spoon; 2 clear, sealable plastic bags or 2 small clear containers with lids; A marker pen and sticky tape for labelling
steps: Lightly dampen both slices of bread with a few drops of water. Do not soak them.
Leave both slices uncovered on a clean plate for about 30 minutes so microorganisms from the air can settle on them.
Place each slice in its own plastic bag or container and seal it firmly. Once sealed, do NOT open it again.
Label each bag with your name and the date.
Put both bags in a warm place away from direct sunlight, such as a kitchen shelf.

activities.title: Making Yoghurt with Helpful Bacteria
activities.materials: 1 cup of fresh milk (cow, goat or camel); 1 tablespoon of plain shop-bought or homemade yoghurt (this contains the living bacteria); A clean container with a lid or a clean cloth cover; A clean spoon; a warm blanket or towel to wrap the container
steps: Ask an adult to help you wash the container with boiling water, then let it cool. This kills unwanted microorganisms.
Warm the milk until it is pleasantly warm to the touch — not hot. Ask an adult to help.
Pour the warm milk into the clean container.
Stir in the tablespoon of yoghurt. This adds the living bacteria that will turn the milk into yoghurt.
Cover the container and wrap it in a blanket to keep it warm. Leave it undisturbed for 6 to 10 hours (overnight works well).
Safety: Keep the sealed bags closed at all times — never open or smell the mould. Throw the sealed bags away, unopened, when the investigation ends, and wash your hands.

activities.title: Does Temperature Affect Decay?
activities.materials: 2 similar slices of bread; A little water; 2 sealable plastic bags or clear containers with lids; A marker pen for labelling; Access to a warm place and a cool place (such as a refrigerator or cool store)
steps: Dampen both slices with the SAME small amount of water so this variable is kept the same.
Seal each slice in its own bag and label them 'Warm' and 'Cool' with the date.
Put the 'Warm' bag in a warm place and the 'Cool' bag in the refrigerator or coolest place you have.
Keep both bags SEALED for the whole experiment.
Each day for 5 to 7 days, look at both slices through the bags and record how much mould has grown.
Safety: Keep the sealed bags closed at all times — never open or smell the mould. Throw the sealed bags away, unopened, when the investigation ends, and wash your hands.

steps: Follow the investigation plan in your experiments book.

steps: Look for an example of microorganisms and decay around your home or outside.

rules.title: Not Every Decomposer Is a Microbe
rules.text: Remember too that not every decomposer is a microorganism. The toadstools growing on a fallen log are the visible part of a fungus, but the hidden threads inside the log are breaking the wood down — so that large fungus is a decomposer even though you can see it easily. And if a slug eats the toadstool, the energy the slug gains can be traced all the way back, through the fungus and the dead wood, to the tree that first captured it from the Sun.

realProblems.answer: Microorganisms (bacteria) grew in the warm rice overnight and made it decay, producing the sour smell. Prevent it by keeping the rice cool (refrigerator/cool store) or covered, or by reheating thoroughly and not leaving it out in the heat.

realProblems.prompt: A farmer near the Jubba River sees that grass grows greener next to cattle dung. Explain how decomposers and dung help the grass grow.
realProblems.answer: Decomposer fungi and bacteria break down the dung and return its nutrients to the soil. The grass roots take up these nutrients, so the grass grows greener and taller near the dung.

realProblems.prompt: Halima makes yoghurt but it sets very slowly. Suggest one change she could make to speed it up, and explain why it would work.
realProblems.answer: Keep the milk warmer (but not hot). Bacteria are living things that grow and work faster in warmth, so the milk turns to yoghurt more quickly. (Also acceptable: add a little more yoghurt starter to add more bacteria.)

realProblems.prompt: Explain why sleeping under a bed net helps protect a child from malaria, referring to the microorganism and how it spreads.
realProblems.answer: Malaria is caused by a protozoan spread by mosquito bites. A bed net stops mosquitoes from biting the sleeping child, so the protozoan cannot be passed on, reducing the risk of malaria.

realProblems.prompt: A family starts a compost pit for fruit peelings and vegetable scraps. Explain what happens in the pit and why the finished compost is good for a garden.
realProblems.answer: Decomposers break down the peelings and scraps, turning them into rich compost full of nutrients. Added to garden soil, these nutrients help plants grow well. It also recycles waste instead of throwing it away.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what a microorganism is and why we need a microscope to study one.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A microorganism is a living thing so small it can only be seen clearly with a microscope. A single one is far smaller than one of our own cells, so our eyes alone cannot see it — only a microscope makes it visible.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the four main kinds of microorganism and give one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Bacteria (e.g. the bacteria in yoghurt); fungi (e.g. yeast or mould); protozoa (e.g. the malaria protozoan); algae (e.g. green algae in pond water).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain how one invisible microorganism can grow into a colony you can see.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: One microorganism divides into two, those two each divide, and so on. In a day or two, one invisible cell becomes millions of cells — a colony — which is large enough to see.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give two examples of useful microorganisms and say what each one does.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Yeast makes dough rise for bread and canjeero; bacteria turn milk into yoghurt and fermented camel milk. (Also acceptable: gut bacteria aid digestion; soil decomposers recycle nutrients.)

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must a Petri dish and agar jelly be sterile before use?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: So that no unwanted microorganisms are already growing on them. If they were not sterile, other microbes would grow and spoil the experiment.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why decomposers are important for keeping plants growing.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Producer: makes its own food from sunlight. Consumer: gets energy by eating other organisms. Herbivore: eats only plants. Carnivore: eats only other animals.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, working at your own pace with help from your AI tutor and your teacher, you will be able to:
I can explain what a microorganism is and why a microscope is needed to see one.
I can name and describe the main kinds of microorganism: bacteria, fungi (including yeast and mould), protozoa and algae, and explain why viruses are treated differently.
I can describe how a single microorganism grows into a colony that is large enough to see.
I can distinguish between microorganisms that are useful to people and those that are harmful.
I can construct and interpret food chains and food webs, using arrows to show the direction of energy transfer.
I can classify organisms as producers, consumers, herbivores, carnivores, predators, prey or decomposers.
I can explain how microorganisms cause decay, and describe the important role of decomposers in returning nutrients to the soil.
